<p class="proj-lead">
A bank that lends to a million households needs two numbers about them: how likely each one is to default, and how likely it is that many default together. This project builds both. A logit estimates the first on 5 million loan-years of US mortgages, the Vasicek model behind the Basel formulas turns it into the second, and a validation on years the model never saw shows what each can and cannot do.
</p>

<p class="proj-meta">Course project, Risk Management and Capital Requirements, Sapienza University of Rome, June to July 2026. Python, pandas, statsmodels, scikit-learn. Data: Freddie Mac Single-Family Loan-Level Dataset, sample edition; only aggregates and model outputs appear here.</p>

## One row per loan and year

The source is 50,000 mortgages for each origination year from 2006 to 2025, about 4.3 GB of monthly text files. I reduced them to one row per loan and calendar year, with the risk drivers read at the start of the year so that nothing from the future leaks in. A loan-year counts as a default if the loan reached 90 or more days past due, or ended in a short sale, a third-party sale or REO; after its first default year a loan leaves the panel. The panel fits in 66 MB, about 65 times smaller than the raw files.

Overall 0.95% of loan-years end in default, and the rate is far from flat: 3.05% in 2009 and 3.42% in 2020, against 0.35 to 0.65% in the other years since 2014.

## 1 · A logit for the PD of a loan

The PD of a loan-year is a logit on four drivers read at origination (credit score, debt-to-income, interest rate, loan-to-value) plus the age of the loan, with a flag for the 13% of loan-years whose debt-to-income is missing. I fitted it on the loan-years up to 2018, 2.74 million of them, and kept 2019 onwards, 2.30 million, for testing. A random split would put 2020 loans in both halves; this way the model has to predict a year it has never seen.

```python
DRIVERS = ["credit_score", "orig_dti", "orig_interest_rate", "orig_ltv", "loan_age"]


def prepare(df, dti_median):
    out = df.copy()
    out["orig_dti_missing"] = out["orig_dti"].isna().astype(int)   # a missing DTI can carry signal by itself
    out["orig_dti"] = out["orig_dti"].fillna(dti_median)           # the TRAIN median, for the test set too
    return out.dropna(subset=DRIVERS)


# fit on the past, predict the future: no shuffling of loan-years
train_raw, test_raw = panel[panel["year"] <= 2018], panel[panel["year"] > 2018]
median = train_raw["orig_dti"].median()
train, test = prepare(train_raw, median), prepare(test_raw, median)

formula = "default ~ " + " + ".join(DRIVERS + ["orig_dti_missing"])
logit = smf.glm(formula, data=train, family=sm.families.Binomial()).fit()
pd_hat = logit.predict(test)                                       # predicted PD, strictly out of time
```

The four origination drivers have the signs credit-risk theory expects, and with millions of rows every coefficient is significant, so what matters is size:

| driver                 | effect on the odds of default     |
| :--------------------- | :-------------------------------- |
| credit score           | × 0.91 for every 10 points        |
| interest rate          | × 2.27 for every percentage point |
| debt-to-income         | × 1.03 for every point            |
| loan-to-value          | × 1.01 for every point            |
| loan age               | × 1.006 for every month           |
| debt-to-income missing | × 1.29                            |

A probit with the same drivers ranks loans the same way and gives nearly the same PDs; its coefficients sit on a different scale, because the logistic distribution is wider than the normal.

## 2 · From one loan to a portfolio

The logit scores each loan on its own and says nothing about how defaults move together. Vasicek's model adds that with one common factor. Each borrower's asset return is $$X = \sqrt{\rho}\,M + \sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon$$, where $$M$$ is the state of the economy and $$\varepsilon$$ is the borrower's own luck; the borrower defaults when $$X$$ falls below $$\Phi^{-1}(PD)$$. Given $$M$$, the default probability of a loan is

$$PD(M) = \Phi\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(PD) - \sqrt{\rho}\,M}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)$$

In a large portfolio the borrowers' own luck averages out, so the loss rate of the portfolio is $$PD(M)$$ itself: the only risk left is the economy's. Basel fixes $$\rho = 0.15$$ for residential mortgages, the value I used. Put $$M$$ at its 99.9% worst case, $$\Phi^{-1}(0.001) = -3.09$$, and the average PD of 0.96% becomes 10.7%, 11.2 times higher. That is also the 99.9% quantile of the portfolio's loss distribution in the lower panel, and the distance from the expected loss to it is what capital has to cover.

```python
def conditional_pd(pd, M, rho):
    """PD of a loan when the economy is in state M (M < 0 is a downturn)."""
    return norm.cdf((norm.ppf(pd) - np.sqrt(rho) * M) / np.sqrt(1 - rho))


def worst_case_pd(pd, rho, q=0.999):
    """The Basel scenario: an economy as bad as it gets once in a thousand years."""
    return conditional_pd(pd, norm.ppf(1 - q), rho)


def loss_cdf(loss, pd, rho):
    """P(loss rate <= loss) for a large portfolio of identical loans."""
    return norm.cdf((np.sqrt(1 - rho) * norm.ppf(loss) - norm.ppf(pd)) / np.sqrt(rho))


def implied_M(observed_rate, pd, rho):
    """The state of the economy that would produce the default rate we actually saw."""
    return (norm.ppf(pd) - np.sqrt(1 - rho) * norm.ppf(observed_rate)) / np.sqrt(rho)
```

Move the slider to see what the correlation does to the same loans: at $$\rho = 0.05$$ the worst case is 4.5%, at $$\rho = 0.30$$ it is 21.9%.

<div class="caption">Top: PD of a loan given the state of the economy. Bottom: the resulting distribution of the loss rate of a large portfolio of identical loans with PD 0.96%, shown as the probability that the loss stays below each level, with its 99.9% quantile marked.</div>

## 3 · Validation on years the model never saw

I checked the logit the way a supervisor would: does it rank loans correctly, are its levels right, and does it hold up over time. On 2019 to 2025 the AUC is 0.653, moderate. The test window leans heavily on one year, 2020, which is 15.6% of the rows but 57% of the defaults; without it the AUC is 0.675. So the COVID year explains part of the modest ranking, not all of it: origination-only drivers do not separate loans sharply in any year.

The levels tell the second half. The mean predicted PD is 0.75% against 0.94% observed, and predictions are more spread out than outcomes: the riskiest tenth of test loans is predicted at 4.1% and defaults at 1.4%, the safest tenth is predicted at 0.04% and defaults at 0.11%. A constant forecast at the observed rate has a Brier score of 0.00927, against 0.00943 for the model, so the value of the model is in the ranking, not in the level.

## 4 · What 2020 does to the model

Year by year the picture is clearer. The logit has no macro factor, so its mean predicted PD is nearly flat from 2019 to 2022 while the default rate jumps to 3.42% in 2020; from 2023 it swings the other way, predicting about twice what happens in 2023 and 2024 and nearly three times in 2025 (1.29% against 0.44%). The interest-rate driver has the largest odds ratio, and the average rate on the loans in the panel rose from 3.8% in 2021 to 5.0% in 2025; the predictions climbed with it while defaults stayed flat.

```plotly
{"data":[{"type":"bar","name":"observed","x":[2019,2020,2021,2022,2023,2024,2025],"y":[0.35059,3.41657,0.65426,0.40803,0.45354,0.55929,0.4437],"marker":{"color":"#e8890c"},"customdata":[0.37,-1.71,-0.14,0.25,0.17,-0.01,0.18],"hovertemplate":"<b>%{x}</b> observed %{y:.2f}%<br>implied M = %{customdata}<extra></extra>"},{"type":"bar","name":"model, mean predicted PD","x":[2019,2020,2021,2022,2023,2024,2025],"y":[0.51592,0.48657,0.44785,0.5104,0.84405,1.12353,1.28953],"marker":{"color":"#2f7de1"},"hovertemplate":"<b>%{x}</b> predicted %{y:.2f}%<extra></extra>"}],"layout":{"paper_bgcolor":"rgba(0,0,0,0)","plot_bgcolor":"rgba(0,0,0,0)","margin":{"l":52,"r":12,"t":14,"b":44},"height":360,"barmode":"group","bargap":0.25,"xaxis":{"tickvals":[2019,2020,2021,2022,2023,2024,2025]},"yaxis":{"ticksuffix":"%","tickformat":".1f","title":{"text":"default rate"}},"legend":{"orientation":"h","x":0,"y":1.1,"yanchor":"bottom"},"annotations":[{"x":2020,"y":3.4166,"text":"implied M = \u22121.71","showarrow":false,"yshift":12,"font":{"size":12}}]},"narrow":{"layout":{"margin":{"l":48,"r":4,"t":14,"b":40}}}}
```

<div class="caption">Default rate observed and predicted by the logit, for each test year. Hover for the systematic factor M implied by each year's default rate.</div>

This is where the Vasicek layer helps. Inverting the formula for each year's default rate gives the state of the economy that would produce it: 2020 comes out at $$M = -1.71$$, the most negative value of the test window, about a one-in-23-year event on the Basel scale. A real shock, and still well inside the 99.9% scenario at $$M = -3.09$$. The COVID spike was driven largely by forbearance, a macro shock with little to do with a borrower's origination quality.

## Can the model be improved?

I added current leverage, categorical drivers, five economically motivated interactions and K-Means borrower segments to the logit (AUC 0.668), re-encoded each driver with weight of evidence (0.714) and trained a random forest (0.692, out of time). All of them are compared on the same test window, so this is exploratory evidence rather than a final ranking. The number that says most is the forest's 0.879 on a random split of the same loans: the 19 points between that and 0.692 are the credit cycle leaking into both halves, which is why the split in this project is by time.
